q: What is Biology?
exp: Biology is the broad science of life and living organisms. Cytology, genetics and ecology are specialised branches within this wider field.

q: Who coined the term “Biology”?
exp: Lamarck and Treviranus are credited with introducing the term Biology. Do not confuse this with Aristotle, who is listed separately as the Father of Biology.

q: Who is known as the Father of Biology?
exp: Aristotle is traditionally called the Father of Biology and is also paired here with Zoology because of his early systematic study and description of animals.

q: What are the Greek roots of the word Biology?
exp: Biology comes from the Greek roots 'Bios' and 'Logos'; together they literally express the idea of the study of life.

q: What does “Bios” mean?
exp: 'Bios' is the Greek root meaning life, and it forms the first part of the word Biology.

q: What does “Logos” mean?
exp: 'Logos' means study or discourse; combined with 'Bios', it gives Biology the meaning 'study of life'.

q: Which statement best describes the overall scope of Biology in living organisms?
a: It studies their structure, function, growth and diversity.
exp: Biology is not limited to a single branch; it examines how living organisms are built, how they function, how they grow and how they differ from one another.

q: Which option contains only living organisms or biological groups commonly studied in Biology?
a: Fungi, algae, bacteria, plants, animals and humans.
exp: Fungi, algae, bacteria, plants, animals and humans are all biological organisms or groups. The other options insert a non-living geological or material category.

q: Which of the following correctly represents examples of microorganisms?
exp: Microbiology deals with microorganisms. Bacteria and protozoa are microscopic, and many fungi and algae are also studied as microorganisms. Therefore, fungi, algae, bacteria and protozoa form the correct group among the given options.

q: Which of the following includes only plant groups or plant forms?
a: Trees, creepers, shrubs, bryophytes and ferns.
exp: Trees, creepers, shrubs, bryophytes and ferns are all plant forms or plant groups. The other sets contain fungi, protozoa or lichens, so they are not exclusively plant groups.

q: Which of the following includes only animals?
a: Earthworm, fish, birds, mammals and snakes.
exp: Earthworm, fish, birds, mammals and snakes are all members of Kingdom Animalia. Each distractor contains at least one non-animal group.

q: Are “coiner of the term Biology” and “Father of Biology” the same fact?
a: No. Lamarck & Treviranus coined the term; Aristotle is the Father of Biology.
exp: No. This is an exam trap: credit Lamarck and Treviranus with the term Biology, while Aristotle is given the title Father of Biology.

q: What does Botany study?
exp: Botany is the branch of biology that studies plants; their structure, growth, reproduction and diversity. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is known as the Father of Botany?
exp: Theophrastus is identified as the Father of Botany because of his early systematic descriptions and classification of plants.

q: Which examples are included under Botany?
a: Algae, bryophytes, ferns, trees, creepers and shrubs.
exp: Botany deals with plants and plant-related groups. The correct set contains only botanical examples, whereas the other sets insert protozoa, an animal, or bacteria.

q: What does Zoology study?
exp: Zoology is the branch of biology that studies animals; their structure, functions, behaviour and diversity. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is known as the Father of Zoology?
exp: Aristotle is traditionally called the Father of Biology and is also paired here with Zoology because of his early systematic study and description of animals.

q: Which examples are included under Zoology?
a: Earthworm, fish, snakes, birds and mammals.
exp: Earthworm, fish, snakes, birds and mammals all belong to Kingdom Animalia; each distractor includes one non-animal group.

q: What does Microbiology study?
exp: Microbiology is the branch of biology that studies microscopic organisms such as bacteria and protozoa. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is known as the Father of Microbiology?
exp: Leeuwenhoek observed microscopic living organisms with powerful simple microscopes, which is why he is associated with Microbiology and Protozoology.

q: Which examples are included under Microbiology?
exp: Cyanobacteria, bacteria and protozoa are microscopic groups commonly encountered in microbiology. Bryophytes, gymnosperms and ferns are macroscopic plant groups.

q: What does Endocrinology study?
exp: Endocrinology is the branch of biology that studies endocrine glands and the hormones they release. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Endocrinology?
exp: Thomas Addison is associated with Endocrinology; his name is linked with disorders involving endocrine glands, especially the adrenal glands.

q: What does Immunology study?
exp: Immunology is the branch of biology that studies the immune system, immunity and defence against foreign agents. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Immunology?
exp: Edward Jenner is linked here with Immunology because his vaccination work demonstrated how immunity can be developed against infectious disease.

q: What does Genetics study?
exp: Genetics is the branch of biology that studies heredity and variation—how traits pass between generations and why individuals differ. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Genetics?
exp: Mendel’s experiments on inheritance established fundamental patterns of heredity, so he is the key scientist associated with Genetics.

q: What does Cytology study?
exp: Cytology is the branch of biology that studies cells, especially their structure, functions and behaviour. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Cytology?
exp: Robert Hooke observed cork under a microscope and introduced the term cell, which explains his association with Cytology.

q: What does Eugenics study?
exp: Historically, eugenics referred to attempts to influence human heredity through selective reproduction. Francis Galton is the scientist most commonly associated with the term; modern science regards eugenic programmes as scientifically flawed and ethically discredited.

q: Who is associated with Eugenics?
exp: Francis Galton is historically associated with Eugenics. For competitive exams, remember the direct pair: Francis Galton ↔ Eugenics.

q: What does Taxonomy study?
exp: Taxonomy is the branch of biology that studies identification, scientific naming and classification of organisms. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Taxonomy?
exp: Linnaeus is central to taxonomy: he is identified as the Father of Taxonomy and is also associated with Binomial Nomenclature.

q: What does Paleontology study?
exp: Paleontology is the branch of biology that studies fossils and evidence of organisms from the geological past. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Paleontology?
exp: George Cuvier is associated here with Paleontology, the branch that reconstructs past life mainly through the study of fossils.

q: What does Embryology study?
exp: Embryology is the branch of biology that studies development from gametes and fertilisation to the embryo. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is known as the Father of Indian Plant Embryology?
exp: Panchanan Maheshwari made major contributions to angiosperm embryology in India and is widely known in Indian exam material as the Father of Indian Plant Embryology.

q: What does Agronomy study?
exp: Agronomy is the branch of biology that studies crop production and soil management. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Agronomy?
exp: Pietro de Crescenzi is associated with Agronomy. The exam link is Agronomy = crop production and soil management.

q: What does Agrostology study?
exp: Agrostology is the specialised study of grasses. Do not confuse it with Anthology (flowers), Spermology (seeds) or Pomology (fruits) in competitive-exam terminology.

q: Who is associated with Agrostology?
exp: Johann Scheuchzer is associated with Agrostology, the specialised study of grasses.

q: What does Anthology study?
exp: In common Indian competitive-exam terminology, Anthology is used for the study of flowers. It should not be confused with the ordinary literary meaning of “anthology”.

q: What does Serpentology study?
exp: Serpentology is the branch of biology that studies snakes. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Serpentology?
exp: Patrick Russell is associated with Serpentology, the specialised study of snakes.

q: What does Protozoology study?
exp: Protozoology is the branch of biology that studies protozoa. This definition separates it from neighbouring branches with different subjects.

q: Who is associated with Protozoology?
exp: Leeuwenhoek observed microscopic living organisms with powerful simple microscopes, which is why he is associated with Microbiology and Protozoology.

q: What is Taxonomy?
a: The identification, naming and classification of living organisms.
exp: Taxonomy organises biodiversity through three linked tasks: identifying an organism, giving it a scientific name and placing it in an appropriate group.

q: Who coined the term “Taxonomy”?
exp: A. P. de Candolle is credited here with coining the term Taxonomy. Do not confuse this with Linnaeus, who is listed as the Father of Taxonomy.

q: Who is known as the Father of Taxonomy?
exp: Linnaeus is central to taxonomy: he is identified as the Father of Taxonomy and is also associated with Binomial Nomenclature.

q: Are the coiner of “Taxonomy” and the Father of Taxonomy the same person?
a: No. A. P. de Candolle coined the term; Carolus Linnaeus is the Father of Taxonomy.
exp: No. A. P. de Candolle coined the term Taxonomy, whereas Carolus Linnaeus is identified as the Father of Taxonomy.

q: Who introduced Binomial Nomenclature?
exp: Linnaeus is central to taxonomy: he is identified as the Father of Taxonomy and is also associated with Binomial Nomenclature.

q: Which book is associated with Linnaeus and Binomial Nomenclature?
exp: Systema Naturae is associated with Linnaeus and systematic classification; remember the scientist–book pair.

q: How many parts are present in a scientific name under Binomial Nomenclature?
exp: A binomial has two parts: the genus name followed by the species epithet. That two-word structure is the defining feature of Binomial Nomenclature.

q: Which two parts make up a binomial scientific name?
exp: A binomial name has two words: the genus name and the specific epithet. Together they identify the species; for example, Homo + sapiens.

q: How are scientific names generally written?
exp: Scientific names are conventionally written in italics when printed, helping distinguish a formal biological name from ordinary text.

q: How is the first letter of the genus written?
exp: The genus begins with a capital letter; this is why Homo in Homo sapiens starts with a capital H.

q: How is the specific epithet written in a binomial scientific name?
a: It begins with a lowercase letter.
exp: The specific epithet begins with a lowercase letter; therefore sapiens in Homo sapiens is written with a small “s”.

q: In Homo sapiens, what is the genus?
exp: In a binomial name the first word is the genus, so Homo is the genus in Homo sapiens.

q: In Homo sapiens, what is the specific epithet?
exp: In a binomial name, the first word is the genus and the second word is the specific epithet. Thus, sapiens is the specific epithet in Homo sapiens.

q: What is the descending taxonomic hierarchy?
a: Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.
exp: The hierarchy runs from the broadest to the most specific category: Kingdom → Phylum/Division → Class → Order → Family → Genus → Species.

q: Which rank is used after Kingdom for animals?
exp: For animals, Phylum comes immediately below Kingdom; plants traditionally use Division at the corresponding level.

q: Which rank is used after Kingdom for plants?
exp: For plants, Division is used immediately below Kingdom; the corresponding animal rank is Phylum.

q: What mnemonic is given for Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species?
a: King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.
exp: 'King Philip Came Over For Good Soup' preserves the initials K-P-C-O-F-G-S, matching the seven taxonomic ranks in order.

q: How are plants preserved in a herbarium?
exp: Herbarium specimens are preserved by drying and pressing plant material so that diagnostic features remain available for identification and study.

q: What is the biological name of Human?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Human is listed as Homo sapiens: Homo is the genus and sapiens is the species epithet.

q: To which family does Human belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Human is Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → Homo sapiens. Reading the family position in that sequence gives Hominidae.

q: To which order does Human belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Human is Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → Homo sapiens. Reading the order position in that sequence gives Primates.

q: To which class does Human belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Human is Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → Homo sapiens. Reading the class position in that sequence gives Mammalia.

q: To which phylum/division does Human belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Human is Chordata → Mammalia → Primates → Hominidae → Homo sapiens. Reading the phylum/division position in that sequence gives Chordata.

q: What is the biological name of House Fly?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, House Fly is listed as Musca domestica: Musca is the genus and domestica is the species epithet.

q: To which family does House Fly belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for House Fly is Arthropoda → Insecta → Diptera → Muscidae → Musca domestica. Reading the family position in that sequence gives Muscidae.

q: To which order does House Fly belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for House Fly is Arthropoda → Insecta → Diptera → Muscidae → Musca domestica. Reading the order position in that sequence gives Diptera.

q: To which class does House Fly belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for House Fly is Arthropoda → Insecta → Diptera → Muscidae → Musca domestica. Reading the class position in that sequence gives Insecta.

q: To which phylum/division does House Fly belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for House Fly is Arthropoda → Insecta → Diptera → Muscidae → Musca domestica. Reading the phylum/division position in that sequence gives Arthropoda.

q: What is the biological name of Mango?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Mango is listed as Mangifera indica: Mangifera is the genus and indica is the species epithet.

q: To which family does Mango belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Mango is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera indica. Reading the family position in that sequence gives Anacardiaceae.

q: To which order does Mango belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Mango is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera indica. Reading the order position in that sequence gives Sapindales.

q: To which class does Mango belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Mango is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera indica. Reading the class position in that sequence gives Dicotyledonae.

q: To which phylum/division does Mango belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Mango is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Sapindales → Anacardiaceae → Mangifera indica. Reading the phylum/division position in that sequence gives Angiospermae.

q: What is the biological name of Wheat?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Wheat is listed as Triticum aestivum: Triticum is the genus and aestivum is the species epithet.

q: To which family does Wheat belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Wheat is Angiospermae → Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Triticum aestivum. Reading the family position in that sequence gives Poaceae.

q: To which order does Wheat belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Wheat is Angiospermae → Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Triticum aestivum. Reading the order position in that sequence gives Poales.

q: To which class does Wheat belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Wheat is Angiospermae → Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Triticum aestivum. Reading the class position in that sequence gives Monocotyledonae.

q: To which phylum/division does Wheat belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Wheat is Angiospermae → Monocotyledonae → Poales → Poaceae → Triticum aestivum. Reading the phylum/division position in that sequence gives Angiospermae.

q: What is the biological name of Potato?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Potato is listed as Solanum tuberosum: Solanum is the genus and tuberosum is the species epithet.

q: To which family does Potato belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Potato is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Solanales → Solanaceae → Solanum tuberosum. Reading the family position in that sequence gives Solanaceae.

q: To which order does Potato belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Potato is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Solanales → Solanaceae → Solanum tuberosum. Reading the order position in that sequence gives Solanales.

q: To which class does Potato belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Potato is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Solanales → Solanaceae → Solanum tuberosum. Reading the class position in that sequence gives Dicotyledonae.

q: To which phylum/division does Potato belong?
exp: The taxonomic sequence for Potato is Angiospermae → Dicotyledonae → Solanales → Solanaceae → Solanum tuberosum. Reading the phylum/division position in that sequence gives Angiospermae.

q: Who proposed the Five Kingdom Classification?
exp: Robert Whittaker proposed the Five Kingdom Classification in 1969, separating organisms into Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

q: In which year was the Five Kingdom Classification proposed?
exp: Robert Whittaker proposed the Five Kingdom Classification in 1969.

q: Which five kingdoms are included in Whittaker’s classification?
a: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.
exp: Whittaker’s system includes Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia, separating organisms by major differences in cell organisation, nutrition and relationship.

q: Which criteria were used for the Five Kingdom Classification?
a: Cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationship.
exp: Whittaker’s five-kingdom classification used cell structure, body organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships as major criteria.

q: Which is the only prokaryotic kingdom among the five kingdoms?
exp: Monera is the only prokaryotic kingdom in this scheme, so its cells lack a true membrane-bound nucleus.

q: Which four kingdoms are eukaryotic?
exp: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia are eukaryotic because their cells possess a true nucleus enclosed by a nuclear membrane.

q: What is the cell type of Kingdom Monera?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Monera has cell type described as prokaryotic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: How is the cell wall of Kingdom Monera described in the NCERT five-kingdom table?
exp: NCERT describes the Monera cell wall generally as non-cellulosic, made of polysaccharides and amino acids. Archaebacteria have a different wall structure, and Mycoplasma completely lacks a cell wall.

q: What is the nuclear membrane of Kingdom Monera?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Monera has nuclear membrane described as absent. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the body organisation of Kingdom Monera?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Monera has body organisation described as unicellular. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nutrition of Kingdom Monera?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Monera has nutrition described as autotrophic and heterotrophic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the reproduction of Kingdom Monera?
a: Binary fission and some sexual reproduction.
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Monera has reproduction described as mainly binary fission. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell type of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has cell type described as eukaryotic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell wall of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has cell wall described as present in a few. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nuclear membrane of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has nuclear membrane described as present. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the body organisation of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has body organisation described as unicellular. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nutrition of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has nutrition described as autotrophic and heterotrophic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the reproduction of Kingdom Protista?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Protista has reproduction described as asexual and sexual. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell type of Kingdom Fungi?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Fungi has cell type described as eukaryotic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell wall of Kingdom Fungi?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Fungi has cell wall described as chitin. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nuclear membrane of Kingdom Fungi?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Fungi has nuclear membrane described as present. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: How is the body organisation of fungi generally described in the five-kingdom scheme?
a: Mostly multicellular / loose tissue; yeast is unicellular.
exp: The five-kingdom table describes fungi as multicellular/loose tissue, while NCERT also notes an important exception: yeasts are unicellular fungi.

q: What is the nutrition of Kingdom Fungi?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Fungi has nutrition described as heterotrophic—saprophytic or parasitic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the reproduction of Kingdom Fungi?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Fungi has reproduction described as spores; asexual and sexual. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell type of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has cell type described as eukaryotic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell wall of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has cell wall described as cellulose. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nuclear membrane of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has nuclear membrane described as present. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the body organisation of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has body organisation described as tissue/organ/organ-system level. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nutrition of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has nutrition described as autotrophic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the reproduction of Kingdom Plantae?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Plantae has reproduction described as vegetative and sexual. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell type of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has cell type described as eukaryotic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the cell wall of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has cell wall described as absent. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nuclear membrane of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has nuclear membrane described as present. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the body organisation of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has body organisation described as tissue/organ/organ-system level. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the nutrition of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has nutrition described as heterotrophic—holozoic or parasitic. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: What is the reproduction of Kingdom Animalia?
exp: In the Whittaker profile used here, Kingdom Animalia has reproduction described as sexual. This is one of the features used to distinguish the five kingdoms.

q: Which kingdom is described in NCERT as having a generally non-cellulosic cell wall made of polysaccharides and amino acids?
exp: In the NCERT five-kingdom table, Monera has a non-cellulosic wall described as polysaccharide + amino acid. Fungi have chitin, Plantae cellulose, and Protista is variable.

q: Which kingdom has a chitinous cell wall?
exp: Chitin is the characteristic wall material of Fungi, distinguishing fungi from cellulose-walled plants.

q: Which kingdom has a cellulose cell wall?
exp: Cellulose is associated with the cell wall of Plantae; fungi have chitin, while animals lack a cell wall.

q: In which kingdom is the cell wall absent?
exp: Animalia lacks a cell wall; animal cells are bounded by a plasma membrane rather than a rigid external wall.

q: In which kingdom is the nuclear membrane absent?
exp: Monera lacks a nuclear membrane because its members are prokaryotic; their genetic material is not enclosed in a true nucleus.

q: Which kingdom includes heterotrophs that may be saprophytic or parasitic?
exp: Fungi are heterotrophs that obtain nutrients from organic matter; include saprophytic and parasitic modes.

q: Which kingdom includes heterotrophs that may be holozoic or parasitic?
exp: Animalia is heterotrophic; animals may obtain food by holozoic nutrition, while some members live as parasites.

q: What important nuclear feature is absent in Monera?
exp: Monerans are prokaryotic, so they do not possess a true membrane-bound nucleus; the nuclear membrane is absent.

q: Which statement best describes Monerans in evolutionary terms?
a: They represent very ancient prokaryotic forms of cellular life.
exp: Monerans are prokaryotes and represent very ancient forms of cellular organisation. They lack a membrane-bound true nucleus and are not eukaryotic or multicellular transition forms.

q: Which archaebacteria are methane-producing?
exp: Methanogens produce methane during anaerobic metabolism, so methane production is the clue that identifies this archaebacterial group.

q: Which of the following is an example of a methanogen?
exp: Methanobacterium is a methanogen. Methanogens are archaebacteria that produce methane during anaerobic metabolism, so methane production is their key identifying feature.

q: Which archaebacteria live in saline marine conditions?
exp: Halophiles are adapted to highly saline environments; the word 'halo' itself gives a useful salt-related clue.

q: Which of the following is an example of a halophile?
exp: Halococcus is a halophile. Halophiles are archaebacteria adapted to environments with very high salt concentration.

q: Which archaebacteria live in hot sulphur springs?
exp: Thermoacidophiles tolerate high temperature and acidic conditions, which is why hot sulphur springs are their characteristic habitat here.

q: Which of the following is an example of a thermoacidophile?
exp: Sulfolobus is a thermoacidophile. Thermoacidophiles tolerate both high temperature and acidic conditions, such as those found around hot sulphur springs.

q: Which eubacterial group is described as blue-green autotrophic bacteria?
exp: Cyanobacteria are photosynthetic prokaryotes traditionally called blue-green algae; the key clues are blue-green colour and autotrophic nutrition.

q: Which pair represents nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria?
exp: Nostoc and Anabaena are nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria. They possess specialised cells called heterocysts that provide suitable conditions for atmospheric nitrogen fixation.

q: Through which specialized cells do Nostoc and Anabaena fix atmospheric nitrogen?
exp: Heterocysts are specialised cells that provide suitable conditions for nitrogen fixation in cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena.

q: What is the key cell-wall feature of Mycoplasma?
exp: Mycoplasma is exceptional among the Monera examples because it lacks a cell wall; this is its key identifying feature.

q: Which statement about Mycoplasma is correct?
a: They completely lack a cell wall; many are pathogenic in animals and plants.
exp: Mycoplasma completely lacks a cell wall. NCERT also notes that they are among the smallest living cells, can survive without oxygen, and many are pathogenic in animals and plants.

q: In lichens, the association between the algal and fungal partners is best described as what?
exp: Lichens are a mutually useful association between an alga and a fungus: the alga prepares food, while the fungus provides shelter and helps absorb water and mineral nutrients.

q: Which two organisms form a lichen?
exp: A lichen is a partnership between a fungus and an alga. The fungus supplies water, minerals and support, while the algal partner makes food by photosynthesis.

q: What does the fungal partner do in a lichen?
exp: The fungal component absorbs water and minerals and provides a protected framework for the algal partner.

q: What does the algal partner do in a lichen?
exp: The algal partner performs photosynthesis and supplies organic food, complementing the fungal partner’s role in water and mineral uptake.

q: Why is lichen called a pioneer organism?
a: It can colonize bare rocks and initiate weathering and succession.
exp: Lichens can establish on bare rock, contribute to rock weathering and help create conditions for later colonisers; therefore they are called pioneer organisms.

q: Lichen is an indicator of which air pollutant?
exp: Lichens are sensitive to sulphur dioxide, so their presence or decline can be used as a biological indicator of SO₂ air pollution.

q: Which dye is obtained from lichens?
exp: Litmus is obtained from certain lichens and is widely used as an acid–base indicator.

q: What is Mycorrhiza?
a: A symbiotic association between fungi and the roots of higher plants.
exp: Mycorrhiza is a mutual association between a fungus and the roots of a higher plant, with both partners gaining from the relationship.

q: How does the fungal partner help the plant in Mycorrhiza?
a: It increases the effective root-absorbing surface and improves mineral uptake, especially phosphorus.
exp: In mycorrhiza, fungal hyphae extend the effective absorbing area of roots and improve uptake of water and minerals, especially phosphorus; the plant supplies organic food to the fungus.

q: How does the plant help the fungal partner in Mycorrhiza?
exp: The plant supplies the fungal partner with shelter and organic nutrition produced through photosynthesis, completing the mutual exchange.

q: Which plants commonly show mycorrhizal association?

q: What is the basic structure of a virus?
a: A protein coat (capsid) + nucleic acid (DNA or RNA).
exp: A virus contains genetic material—DNA or RNA—surrounded by a protein coat called the capsid. The key contrast is virus = nucleic acid + protein coat.

q: Viruses are best described as which type of parasite?
exp: Viruses reproduce only inside living host cells by using host-cell machinery; therefore they are obligate intracellular parasites.

q: Which feature best explains why viruses are described as a link between living and non-living forms?
a: They replicate inside living cells but remain inert and can be crystallised outside them.
exp: Inside a living host cell, viruses use host machinery to replicate; outside the host they are metabolically inert and can form crystalline structures. This combination gives them living as well as non-living features.

q: Who discovered viroids?

q: What is a viroid made of?

q: Do viroids have a protein coat?

q: How are viroids best described structurally?

exp: Viroids are very small infectious RNA agents that lack the protein coat found in viruses. They consist of naked, circular single-stranded RNA.

q: Which disease is associated with viroids in Chrysanthemum?

q: Who discovered prions?

q: What is a prion made of?
exp: A prion is an infectious protein particle. Its defining feature is protein without DNA or RNA.

q: Do prions contain nucleic acid?
exp: No. Prions are unusual infectious agents made of protein only, with no nucleic acid.

q: Which prion disease occurs in sheep and goats?

q: Which human diseases are caused by prions?

q: Which acellular structure has nucleic acid plus a protein coat?

q: Which acellular structure contains RNA only?

q: Which acellular structure contains protein only?
exp: Prion is the protein-only acellular infectious agent; viroids are RNA-only, while viruses contain nucleic acid plus a protein coat.

q: Virus structure?
exp: A virus contains genetic material—DNA or RNA—surrounded by a protein coat called the capsid. The key contrast is virus = nucleic acid + protein coat.

q: Tiger biological name?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Tiger is listed as Panthera tigris: Panthera is the genus and tigris is the species epithet.

q: Lion biological name?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Lion is listed as Panthera leo: Panthera is the genus and leo is the species epithet.

q: Leopard biological name?
exp: The leopard is Panthera pardus: Panthera is the genus and pardus is the specific epithet.

q: Rice biological name?

q: Wheat biological name?
exp: In binomial nomenclature, Wheat is listed as Triticum aestivum: Triticum is the genus and aestivum is the species epithet.

q: Potato biological name?

q: Tea biological name?

q: Human biological name?
